---
title: "1 Homework: data and leakage, with an agent"
---

Three exercises for after Session 1. In each you direct an AI coding agent — any agent that
can read files and run commands in your Codespace — and then check what it produced against
the repository. The skill is not getting an answer; it is knowing whether the answer is right.

**Before you start.** Work on `main` (`git checkout main`), at the repository's root. Each
answer goes in `wiki/homework/_answers/<ID>.md`; that folder is ignored by git, so nothing you
write there is committed or shared. Scripts the agent writes belong in a scratch folder
outside the repository. Each self-check recomputes every number itself and never trusts one
pasted into your answer:

```bash
python -m wiki.homework.check <ID>
```

Each solution below was written by running the exercise with an agent (Claude Code) in this
repository, including where its first attempt went wrong. Try the exercise before you open
it.

## H1.1 Ask: which columns leak? {#h1-1}

**Kind:** Ask. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.1.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.1.md).
**Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H1.1.md`.

**Goal.** Have the agent go through the columns of the applicant file and decide, for each,
whether it would exist when the credit decision is made — before it reads the deny-list. Then
have it compare its list with `LEAKAGE_COLUMNS` in `shared/config.py`
([D2, leakage controls](../mdd/d2-data.qmd#leakage-controls)).

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H1.1` — it reads the deny-list and the file's
columns itself, and wants one `LEAK:` line for each deny-listed column of
`businesses.parquet`, no other column, a reason on every line, and the deny-list exactly as
committed.

**The trap.** Two of them. An agent that reads the deny-list first returns it, and you learn
nothing about whether it can tell a leak from a predictor. And predictive is not leaky:
`net_income` and `requested_amount` predict default because the generator builds them from
`annual_revenue`, but they are on the application. A third, smaller one: the deny-list names
two columns that are not in this file at all.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written — in a fresh agent session, for the
reason below.

**The agent's answer** (excerpt):

> - **LEAK:** `pd_default_origination` — the generator's true probability of default; no
>   bank observes it, at decision time or ever.
> - **LEAK:** `default` — the outcome the model predicts; it is known only months after the
>   loan is booked.
> - **LEAK:** `booked` — whether the loan was funded: decided after the credit decision, and
>   in this generator drawn from the true PD.
> - **LEAK:** `risk_based_rate` — the quoted rate. The generator builds it as cost of funds
>   plus the true PD times LGD plus opex and margin, plus a small noise term: the true PD,
>   rescaled.
>
> The deny-list's other two columns, `deterioration_next_6_12mo` and `line_increase_good`,
> live in `portfolio.parquet` only: later outcomes on booked accounts.

**Where it first went wrong.** The list was right first time, and the check passed. The
reasons were not. The first draft said `risk_based_rate` was "set from a risk view of the
borrower, so a model fed it is reading another model's answer", and that `booked` was
"decided after the credit decision". Both are plausible about a real bank and say nothing
about this data. Reading `shared/data_generator.py` showed the stronger reason for each:

```python
    risk_based_rate = (                                   # shared/data_generator.py, verbatim
        MARKET["cost_of_funds"]
        + pd_true * MARKET["lgd"]
        + MARKET["opex_rate"]
        + MARKET["base_margin"]
        + rng.normal(0.0, 0.003, n)
    ).round(4)

    approve_logit = 2.0 - 6.0 * pd_true + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, n)
```

Both columns are the true PD in disguise. The check confirms the list, not the reasons; the
reasons are yours to judge.

The blind was not blind, either: the agent had read `shared/config.py` earlier in the same
session, so step 1 of the card could not be honoured. That is why the card says to start a
fresh session.

**Rehearsed.** A `LEAK:` line for `line_increase_good` fails with "it is on the deny-list, but
it lives in portfolio.parquet only"; one for `net_income` fails as "not on the deny-list".
:::

## H1.2 Build: the ladder's middle rung {#h1-2}

**Kind:** Build. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.2.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.2.md).
**Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H1.2.md`.

**Goal.** Have the agent fit the leakage probe's honest model and the same model with the
generator's true PD added, report both held-out AUCs, and say in one sentence why the second
cannot ship. Then delete the probe.

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H1.2` — it refits both rungs and compares them with
your answer (three or four decimals, or as a percentage), looks for a sentence saying the
true PD does not exist at decision time, fails if a script that fits a model on the true PD
is left untracked in the repository, and fails if the deny-list has moved.

**The trap.** The number looks fine. The middle rung is not a suspicious near-perfect AUC; it
is the kind of number a good scorecard reaches, so a review that reads only metrics passes
it. A second trap is the recipe: another seed, another split or more trees give another
number, and then the gain over the honest rung means nothing.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> Same recipe for both models, AUC on the {{< var score.n_test >}} held-out applicants:
> honest, {{< var leakage.honest.auc >}}; with `pd_default_origination` added,
> {{< var leakage.truepd.auc >}} — a gain of about {{< var leakage.truepd.gain >}}. Nothing
> about the second number looks wrong. It cannot ship, because the true PD does not exist at
> decision time: no bank observes it, so in production the model would be fed something else.

**Where it first went wrong.** It followed the lab sheet too literally. The sheet names the
script `leakage_probe.py`, so the agent wrote it at the repository's root, ran it and wrote
the answer. The check failed: "delete the probe now you have its number:
leakage_probe.py". The script's first line in the lab sheet says the same — run it, read
the numbers, then delete the file — and the agent had skipped it. A probe left in a repository
is a leak waiting for someone to import it. Deleting it passed the check.

**Rehearsed.** An answer that quotes the true PD's own AUC over all applicants,
{{< var ceiling.truepd_all >}}, instead of the rung fails, and the check names it as the
nearest number in the answer: a true number from a different experiment.
:::

## H1.3 Catch: "leaking the true PD gives AUC ≈ 1.0" {#h1-3}

**Kind:** Catch. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.3.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H1.3.md)
— it carries the transcript to catch. **Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H1.3.md`.

**Goal.** An agent's summary of the probe says that leaking the true PD pushes the AUC to
about 1.0, and that leakage is therefore easy to catch. Find what is wrong with it, have the
ladder measured, and write the correction: a table giving each leaked column its AUC, and the
reason even the true PD cannot rank defaults perfectly.

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H1.3` — it refits the ladder, then wants the table
row naming the true PD to carry the true-PD rung's AUC, the row naming `default` to carry the
label rung's, and a sentence outside the table saying why the true PD cannot reach 1.0. The
check reads the table, not your prose about the transcript, so the sentence on what "easy to
catch" gets wrong is yours to judge.

**The trap.** The transcript's numbers are real; it pins them on the wrong columns. The 1.0
belongs to the label. A correction that only changes the digits misses the lesson: the leak
that ships is the one whose number looks like a good model.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written.

**The agent's correction** (excerpt):

> | Leaked column | AUC |
> |---|---|
> | none — the honest model | {{< var leakage.honest.auc >}} |
> | `pd_default_origination`, the true PD | {{< var leakage.truepd.auc >}} |
> | `default`, the label itself | {{< var leakage.label.auc >}} |
>
> The near-perfect AUC comes from leaking the label. Why the true PD cannot reach 1.0: in
> `shared/data_generator.py` each default is drawn from it, `default = rng.binomial(1, pd_true)`.
> A loan with a low true PD still defaults sometimes and one with a high PD often does not,
> so even a perfect estimate ranks the outcomes imperfectly. On the same held-out rows the
> true PD itself, used directly as the score, has an AUC of {{< var leakage.truepd.alone_auc >}}.

**Where it nearly went wrong.** The check passed first time. The trap was in the last
sentence. The facts already held an AUC for the true PD — {{< var ceiling.truepd_all >}}, over
all applicants — which is *below* the rung. Set beside {{< var leakage.truepd.auc >}}, it says
a model leaking the truth beats the truth. It does not: the two numbers are measured on
different samples. On the rung's own held-out rows the true PD scores
{{< var leakage.truepd.alone_auc >}}, above the rung, as expected. Compare an AUC only with
another measured on the same rows.

**Rehearsed.** The transcript's own version — the label's AUC on the true-PD row and the
true PD's on the label's — fails both table checks.
:::

## Check your own work

After any exercise, `python verify.py` should still pass. If it does not, the agent changed
something it was told not to: `git status` shows what, and `git checkout -- <path>` puts it
back.
